agent_explanations_oldest_first.text:
The pass returned 335 texts with layer-20 states. Now comes the block-126 analysis, applied per group. First the onset, novel and in-loop newlines are found. Each hidden state at an onset or novel newline is centred on the mean of novel newlines sharing the same next token, pooled over all groups, so every group is measured from one common reference.

For each group I report three numbers:
- **gap_sd:** how far onset newlines sit above that group's own novel newlines along dclean, in SD units of the pooled novel lines.
- **mean onset log-prob:** the log-probability of the first token of the repeated line.
- **share above novel P90:** the share of onsets above the 90th percentile of novel lines.

If gap_sd for new loops is similar to the persistent loops', they share the onset channel.

The new loops differ from the persistent ones in three ways.
- **Weaker onset signal:** their onsets sit only 0.39 SD above their own novel lines along dclean, against 0.86 SD for persistent loops. Only 22% exceed the novel-line 90th percentile, against 36%.
- **Higher baseline:** their novel lines already start higher (+0.15 SD, against −0.29 for finished answers).
- **Stronger pull of the repeated line:** they enter repetition with a more confident first token (log-prob −0.34 against −0.47).

So the edit-created loops are less driven by the onset direction C dampens. They look like a drift: the whole trajectory stays elevated, and repetition takes over from a weaker signal. Also, 31 of the 105 newly cut answers have no exact repeated line at all, so they run out of tokens without a loop.

Before writing this up, I'll check how solid the gap difference is with a bootstrap over texts (resampling whole answers, a plain statistic). I'll also describe the 31 no-onset cases: answer length in lines, share of distinct lines, and whether a "####" marker ever appears. A difference beyond about 2 SE supports "a partly different route". Otherwise I'll report it as suggestive only.

The difference holds up. Edit-created loops enter with an onset signal 0.47 ± 0.15 SD weaker than persistent loops (bootstrap over texts; no resample reversed it, p ≈ 0.001). So they are only partly driven by the dclean channel that C targets.

The 31 newly cut answers without an exact repeat have a median of 21 substantial lines. All their lines are distinct, and none reaches a "####" marker. That suggests near-repeats (the same step with changing numbers) or long drifting reasoning rather than verbatim loops. To tell the two apart, I'll print the last ~250 characters of two such answers. I'll also count, over all 31, answers with a fuzzy loop: the same line once digits are stripped, repeated 3 or more times. If most are fuzzy loops, the new failures are counting-style loops that the exact-repeat onset detector misses. If not, they are open-ended drift.

The 31 "no-onset" answers are loops too, of two forms the newline-based detector misses.
- **Within-line repetition:** one example repeats "= $1400.00 + $600.00" endlessly on a single line.
- **Numbered-list loops:** the same item recurs with an incrementing number ("20. **Calculate the time...").

18 of the 31 have a digit-stripped line repeated 3 or more times (median 8), and the rest are mostly within-line loops. So almost every newly cut answer is a genuine loop, not open-ended drift.

To show whether C itself makes these repetitions more likely, I'll spend one pass scoring the same 335 texts with the ORIGINAL model, which the tool returns as token log-probs and layer-20 states. Then I compare, per group and at the same onset positions:
- the log-prob of the first repeated token under each model;
- the onset projection on dclean.

If the original assigns a clearly lower log-prob at the new-loop onsets but not at the persistent ones, C directly raised the pull of repetition there, which identifies a specific side effect. If both models score them alike, those trajectories were already fragile and C only steered generation into them earlier. I'm recording this in the notes first.
